questions.question: The first commercial Christmas card went on sale in London in 1843. Who commissioned it?
questions.explanation: Henry Cole was a civil servant, a Penny Post reformer and later the founding director of what became the V&A. Too busy to write his usual Christmas letters, he commissioned the artist John Callcott Horsley to design a card. About a thousand were printed and sold at a shilling each. The centre panel showed a family raising glasses of wine, a small child among them, which drew complaints from temperance campaigners. Louis Prang, the German-born Boston lithographer, popularised the card in America in the 1870s.

questions.question: In 1897 eight-year-old Virginia O’Hanlon wrote to ask whether Santa Claus was real. Which newspaper printed the reply, “Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus”?
questions.explanation: The editorial ran unsigned in the New York Sun on 21 September 1897, so not at Christmas at all. Its author, the former Civil War correspondent Francis Pharcellus Church, was named only after his death in 1906. It went on to become the most reprinted editorial in the history of English-language newspapers.

questions.question: Long before Prince Albert, which German-born queen set up one of the first documented Christmas trees in England, at Windsor in 1800?
questions.explanation: Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, wife of George III, decorated a yew tree for a children’s party at Queen’s Lodge, Windsor. For decades the custom stayed largely aristocratic. That changed in 1848, when the Illustrated London News printed an engraving of Victoria, Albert and their children around a tabletop tree. In 1850 the American magazine Godey’s Lady’s Book reprinted the image with the royal regalia and Albert’s moustache removed, turning the family into a respectable American household.

questions.question: The Christmas cracker grew out of a sugared-almond bon-bon wrapped in a twist of paper. Which London confectioner developed it?
questions.explanation: Tom Smith, inspired by French bon-bons, began selling paper-wrapped sweets with love mottoes tucked inside around 1847. The crack, a chemically treated strip of card that snaps when pulled, came later and was reputedly inspired by the crackle of a log fire. His sons eventually dropped the sweet altogether in favour of paper hats, trinkets and the dreadful jokes.

questions.question: In 1647 England formally abolished Christmas as a feast day. Who was responsible?
questions.explanation: In June 1647 the Puritan-dominated Long Parliament abolished Christmas, Easter and Whitsun as feasts, which set off pro-Christmas riots in Canterbury and elsewhere that December. Cromwell usually takes the blame, but he did not become Lord Protector until 1653. Laud had been executed in 1645. Christmas came back legally with the Restoration in 1660.

questions.question: “Stille Nacht” was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 in Oberndorf, near Salzburg. What instrument accompanied it?
questions.explanation: The assistant priest Joseph Mohr wrote the words, and the schoolteacher and organist Franz Xaver Gruber set them for two solo voices, choir and guitar. The two men performed it together at St Nicholas Church. The familiar story that mice had chewed through the organ bellows is a later embellishment with no contemporary evidence behind it.

questions.question: In the first printing of “A Visit from St. Nicholas” in 1823, the last two reindeer were not called Donner and Blitzen. What were they called?
questions.explanation: The poem appeared anonymously in the Troy Sentinel on 23 December 1823 with “Dunder and Blixem”, Dutch-flavoured words for thunder and lightning. Clement Clarke Moore changed them to “Donder and Blitzen” when he put the poem in his collected Poems of 1844, and “Donner” came later still. Descendants of Henry Livingston Jr. have long argued that he, not Moore, was the real author.

questions.question: Thomas Nast’s first Santa Claus for Harper’s Weekly, dated January 1863, shows Santa doing what?
options: Handing out gifts to Union soldiers
Driving his sleigh over the Capitol
Checking a ledger of good children
questions.explanation: “Santa Claus in Camp” ran on the cover of the 3 January 1863 issue. It shows Santa in a stars-and-stripes jacket giving out presents to Union troops, while one gift is a puppet of Jefferson Davis with a rope around its neck. Nast went on to draw Santa for Harper’s for more than twenty years, and those drawings settled the North Pole workshop and the naughty-or-nice ledger in American minds.

questions.question: In “The Twelve Days of Christmas”, the verses are cumulative: each day the true love sends that day’s gift and repeats every earlier one. How many gifts arrive in total?
questions.explanation: Day one brings 1 gift, day two brings 3 and day three brings 6. The daily totals are the triangular numbers, and over twelve days they add up to 364, one for every day of the year bar one. The swans and the geese arrive most often, at 42 apiece.

questions.question: In A Christmas Carol, what does the Ghost of Christmas Present show the Cratchits eating for Christmas dinner?
questions.explanation: Mrs Cratchit’s goose is a modest bird stretched across a large family with apple sauce and mashed potatoes. Once reformed, Scrooge sends them the prize turkey from the poulterer’s, “twice the size of Tiny Tim”. For most of the Victorian era goose was the usual celebration bird. Turkey became the standard English Christmas dinner only in the twentieth century.

questions.question: Tinsel was first made in Nuremberg in the early 1600s. What was it made from?
questions.explanation: Real silver was hammered thin and cut into strips. It glittered beautifully but tarnished quickly by candlelight. Cheaper alloys followed, then lead foil, which the United States phased out in the 1970s over safety concerns, then aluminium and today’s PVC. The word comes from the Old French estincele, meaning “spark”.

questions.question: The poinsettia is named after Joel Roberts Poinsett, who sent cuttings home to South Carolina in the 1820s. What was he doing in Mexico?
options: Serving as the first US Minister to Mexico
Surveying the Texas border for the Army
questions.explanation: Poinsett was an amateur botanist as well as a diplomat, and he later served as Secretary of War under Martin Van Buren. The Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxochitl and used its bracts for red dye. In the United States, 12 December is National Poinsettia Day, marking the anniversary of his death in 1851.

questions.question: In December 1882 a New York parlour displayed the first electrically lit Christmas tree. Whose was it?
questions.explanation: Edward Hibberd Johnson, Edison’s partner and vice-president of the Edison Electric Light Company, hand-wired 80 red, white and blue bulbs onto a tree that slowly revolved. A Detroit newspaper reported it. Electric tree lights stayed a rich man’s novelty for years, and candles, with all their fire risk, remained common for decades.

questions.question: “Jingle Bells” was first published in 1857 under what title?
questions.explanation: James Lord Pierpont published it in Boston in 1857. The lyrics never mention Christmas; it is a winter sleighing song. Medford, Massachusetts, and Savannah, Georgia, both claim it. In December 1965 it became the first song played in space, when the Gemini 6 astronauts Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford performed it on a smuggled harmonica and a handful of bells.

questions.question: “Good King Wenceslas looked out, on the Feast of Stephen.” On what date is that feast?
questions.explanation: The Feast of St Stephen, the first Christian martyr, falls on 26 December, Boxing Day. John Mason Neale wrote the words in 1853 and set them to “Tempus adest floridum”, a spring carol from the 1582 Finnish collection Piae Cantiones. The real Wenceslas was a tenth-century Duke of Bohemia; he was given the title of king only after his death.

questions.question: What did the old greeting “wassail” originally mean?
questions.explanation: It comes from Old English wes hal and Old Norse ves heill, literally “be whole”, and the proper reply was “drinkhail”. Over time the word came to mean the drink itself (hot ale or cider with spices, sugar and roasted apples), carolling door to door with a bowl, and, in cider country, a Twelfth Night ritual of toasting the apple trees for a good harvest.

questions.question: The Roman festival of Saturnalia, with its feasting, gift-giving and topsy-turvy role reversals, began on which date?
questions.explanation: Saturnalia opened on 17 December, today’s door, and by the late Republic it had stretched to a week. Togas gave way to casual dining clothes and the felt cap of freed slaves, gambling was allowed in public, and people exchanged small gifts such as wax candles and the clay figurines called sigillaria. Catullus called it “the best of days”.

questions.question: Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker premiered in December 1892. Where?
questions.explanation: It opened at the Mariinsky on 18 December 1892 (6 December in the Russian calendar of the day), on a double bill with his opera Iolanta, and the reception was lukewarm. For the Sugar Plum Fairy, Tchaikovsky used the celesta, an instrument he had come across in Paris, and asked his publisher to keep it quiet so that rival composers could not use it first. Its place as a Christmas fixture is largely an American, post-war development.

questions.question: A Christmas Carol was first published on 19 December, today’s date. In which year?
questions.explanation: Chapman & Hall issued it on 19 December 1843, but Dickens paid the costs himself and insisted on a lavish edition, with gilt edges and hand-coloured plates by John Leech, priced at five shillings. The first 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve, yet the expense left him with a disappointing profit of about £230.

questions.question: Dickens divided A Christmas Carol into five parts. What did he call them?
questions.explanation: Keeping up the idea of a carol, each chapter is a “stave”, an old word for a verse or stanza of a song. He carried the joke into his later Christmas books: The Chimes is divided into “quarters” and The Cricket on the Hearth into “chirps”.

questions.question: In Norse myth, a dart of mistletoe kills which god? It was the one thing his mother never asked to swear not to harm him.
questions.explanation: Frigg made fire, water, metals, stones, beasts and plants all swear never to harm her son Baldr, but she passed over the mistletoe as too young. Loki made a dart from it and guided the throw of the blind god Höðr. Kissing under the mistletoe is much later: it is first recorded in England in the eighteenth century, and by custom a berry was picked for each kiss until none were left.

questions.question: Haddon Sundblom’s Coca-Cola advertisements, from 1931, are often credited with giving Santa his red suit. Is that so?
options: No. Red-suited Santas were common decades earlier.
Yes. The red was chosen to match the brand.
No. The red suit came from 1950s department stores.
questions.explanation: Santa wears red on Puck magazine covers from the early 1900s and on a great many Victorian and Edwardian cards. Other cards show him in green, brown or blue, and that is where the myth gets its foothold. What Sundblom did fix was the warm, rotund, grandfatherly face, modelled at first on a retired salesman friend and later on himself.

questions.question: Every year since 1947 the Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square has been a gift from which city?
questions.explanation: Oslo sends a Norway spruce from the forests around the city each year. It is a thank-you for Britain’s support during the Second World War, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government in exile were based in London. The tree is dressed in the Norwegian manner, with vertical strings of plain white lights. Bergen sends a tree of its own each year to Newcastle upon Tyne.

questions.question: On Christmas Eve 1906, Reginald Fessenden is said to have made one of the first radio broadcasts of voice and music, from Brant Rock, Massachusetts. What did he play on the violin?
questions.explanation: By Fessenden’s own later account, he played Adolphe Adam’s “O Holy Night” on the violin, sang the last verse and read from the Gospel of Luke, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men”, for ships’ wireless operators at sea. No contemporary record survives, so historians treat the story with caution, but it makes a fitting close to the calendar. A merry Christmas to you.
